title: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says
description: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks h
body: Three violent attacks at Polish schools this week were driven by the "glorification of violence" online, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said.The attacks have left one woman dead and others injured, including children."These are very often spontaneous actions inspired by online activity," Tusk said on Sunday, during a crisis meeting with security services. Police have arrested 117 people across the country for possession knives or other weapons, or for threatening to attack schools or fellow students, after searching tens of thousands of schools.A woman was arrested on Saturday after injuring three people while attacking a 17-year-old girl at an educational institution in the capital, Warsaw.It came a day after thousands of police visited schools across Poland, following two stabbing attacks earlier in the week, one of which led to the killing of a female caretaker."We are not dealing with any group organized on a big scale," Tusk said on Sunday. "In the past years and months, we have noted - globally and in Poland - a rise in the fascination with violence," he added.The prime minister said the attacks were acts of "nihilistic violence" associated with the extreme right."Some of the people detained are active in the ultraright environment," he said, adding that police had noticed a rise in online searches of Nazi content as well as of "mass killers who have become idols online".On Wednesday, a 19-year-old student attacked and injured nine people at a vocational school in the central Polish province of Mazovian.A day later, the 37-year-old caretaker was killed after a 15-year-old entered a primary school in Leszczydół-Nowiny, north of Warsaw.Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński also said a 17-year-old was detained in the town of Sierpc, north-west of Warsaw, after allegedly stating "on school grounds that he planned to do something... dangerous - that he intended to harm someone".Thousands of Polish ‌police officers visited schools nationwide to try to reassure pupils after the stabbings sparked rumours of a "Bloody Friday" of more attacks stemming from a supposed online challenge.Meanwhile, Polish security services convened a special meeting on Sunday after receiving information about a potential attack on Tusk and Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, a spokesperson said.A special services spokesman said officials were treating the threat as "deadly serious".

schema.headline: Poland stabbings driven by online glorification of violence, Tusk says

title: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge
description: First Test, Durban (day three of five)Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54Australia lead by 139 runsScoreca
body: First Test, Durban (day three of five)Australia 390 & 33-0: Maddinson 17*South Africa 284: Bedingham 49; Cummins 3-54Australia lead by 139 runsScorecardAustralia's modern Test side remain a fascinating one to unpick.Viewed by many in England as there for the taking in last winter's Ashes despite a 4-1 win, they are also labelled too old by many observers at home.The victims of recent shock defeats by West Indies and Bangladesh, they are still unbeaten in their past nine Test series.But while their struggling batting line-up was bailed out by Matt Renshaw across the first two days of the first Test in Durban, they took control over South Africa on day three in an all-too familiar way.Nine years after they first appeared together as Australia's bowling quartet, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood, Pat Cummins and Nathan Lyon produced their latest relentless performance to dismiss South Africa for 284. There was even some magic from Steve Smith thrown in too.Cummins took three wickets, Starc, Hazlewood and Lyon two apiece, in doing so brushing off any doubts about their effectiveness at the start of a run of Tests against the world Test champions, in-form New Zealand, India and England.The result is Australia's fabled foursome now have 607 wickets in Tests in which they have played as a quartet.The next most successful bowling four-pronged attack is James Anderson, Stuart Broad, Ben Stokes and Moeen Ali, who took 415 wickets in their 31 Tests together for England.Much has been made of Australia's ageing side and a perceived lack of succession planning.At 37, Starc is the oldest of the three quicks but his average pace of 141.21km/h in 2026 is higher than any of his past three years. He is also averaging his most swing in a calendar year since 2015.The concern for Australia comes when they are not fit, with Hazlewood having missed all five of last winter's Ashes Tests and Cummins four.Australia's issue right now is keeping each of their quartet on the field, because they appear as good as ever.At 33-0, Australia lead South Africa by 139 runs.Even with bad light halting play early again, they should have the time to press home an advantage across the Test's final two days.

schema.headline: Australia v South Africa: Pace attack and Steve Smith put tourists in charge

title: Singapore Grand Prix result: Max Verstappen wins from Charles Leclerc with Kimi Antonelli third
description: Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second dominant victory within a week as he secured his first win in the Singapore Grand Prix.Verstappen fought off
body: Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second dominant victory within a week as he secured his first win in the Singapore Grand Prix.Verstappen fought off an attack from Ferrari's Charles Leclerc off the start line to control the race from start to finish.The win followed his and Red Bull's maiden victory of the year in Malaysia last weekend and sprint race success in Singapore on Saturday, confirming the team's re-emergence as a major force.Leclerc took second as team-mate Lewis Hamilton finished sixth after a baffling strategy that was a consequence of the Briton choosing not to pit when asked.Hamilton, trying to last out on a set of soft tyres for a mammoth 44 laps, lost out in the closing laps to Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli and the McLarens of Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri.Antonelli's third place combined with team-mate George Russell finishing only ninth after starting from 19th extends the Italian's championship lead to 102 points.That means it is possible for Antonelli to clinch his first world title at the next race, the United States Grand Prix on 25 October.To become champion in Austin, he would need to win the race with Russell finishing ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower.The key stories of the race were:Verstappen's dominance reviving memories of his pomp during his title-winning eraA confusing day at Ferrari with regard to strategyAntonelli closing on the world titleVerstappen knew he needed to get into the first corner first to try to win the race, given the difficulty of overtaking in Singapore, and he fought tooth and nail to make sure he did.Leclerc got a better start than Verstappen off the line and challenged down the inside as they approached Turn One.But Verstappen squeezed him tight towards the pit wall and with their entry to the first corner so compromised, Leclerc eventually backed off and the four-time champion could claim the corner.Verstappen, Leclerc and Hamilton ran nose to tail for the first four laps before the seven-time champion began to drop back from about lap five.Leclerc stuck within a second of Verstappen for a further five laps before the Red Bull began to edge away from him as well.From then on, Verstappen continued to build his lead and never looked like being beaten as he motored away into the distance."I think the last few races have been really positive for us and it is just great to see and we have a lot of motivation in the team to try and deliver even more results," said Verstappen. "It is a really good group of people - I really enjoy working with them and hopefully we can have a bit more fun until the end of the year."In the interviews immediately after the race, Antonelli was told he can win the title in Austin and responded: "Can I? Really? Let's not worry about that, let's try to do the best weekend possible and finish the job."Hamilton had started on the medium tyres while Verstappen and Leclerc chose the softs. Despite his theoretically more durable tyres, the Briton pitted on lap 18 to switch to the softs, while Leclerc waited until lap 24 to swap his softs for mediums.Leclerc came out of the pits from his stop just ahead of Hamilton, who had stronger pace on his softer tyres.Yet Ferrari chose not to order Leclerc to let Hamilton through to maximise his pace, a decision that was questioned by Hamilton from the car.A virtual safety car was called on lap 39 and Leclerc and Antonelli, who had chased the Ferraris closely from the start from his fourth place on the grid, took the opportunity for a cheap pit stop - it takes 10 seconds less to stop under a safety car than under racing conditions.Yet Hamilton, despite having older tyres, did not stop, a decision that promoted him to second behind Verstappen.As Leclerc was catching Hamilton, the Briton was told he needed to stop again; he pushed back to suggest he try to go to the end, but was told they were six laps short to make it in terms of tyre life.Leclerc soon caught Hamilton and passed him on lap 46 and set off after Verstappen, but could get no closer than 7.3 seconds to the Red Bull.Hamilton never did stop, but as his tyres lost grip he fell back into the clutches of Norris and Antonelli.A passing attempt by Norris on lap 54 with eight to go saw Hamilton run off track and take to the escape road at Turn One, but as he did, Antonelli grabbed the chance to pass the McLaren, and then Hamilton later on the same lap.Norris followed him through, and now Hamilton fell back towards the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri, who passed him on the final lap after a resolute attempted defence from Hamilton.It was Hamilton's call not to stop and he apologised for it on the slowing down lap.Russell's fight back through the field took him up to seventh as he delayed his pit stop as long as possible.But after dropping back to 10th behind Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Alpine's Pierre Gasly, he passed Gasly after trailing him for 10 laps or so, but could not make it past Hulkenberg, who was himself chasing Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson.Red Bull's Isack Hadjar took the final point in 10th after starting from the back.

schema.headline: Singapore Grand Prix result: Max Verstappen wins from Charles Leclerc with Kimi Antonelli third

title: Northern Lights dazzles skies across the UK
description: Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / Jonny GiosImage caption, Kendal in Cumbria played host to breathtaking scenes on SaturdayUpdated 7 hours agoResid
body: Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / Jonny GiosImage caption, Kendal in Cumbria played host to breathtaking scenes on SaturdayUpdated 7 hours agoResidents across the UK were left stunned as the sky was illuminated by the spectacular colours of the Northern Lights on Friday and Saturday evenings.The natural phenomenon, known as the Aurora Borealis, is the result of increased solar activity.Such occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland, but particularly strong activity levels meant they could be seen across Wales and as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent on Saturday night.The Met Office has said sightings could continue to be possible during clear skies until Tuesday.Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / Simon Luckman 1988Image caption, The phenomenon was visible as a pink haze in Winterton-on-Sea, Norfolk, on FridayImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / Isle ExplorerImage caption, Owston Ferry in North Lincolnshire was graced by a stunning purple haze Image source, BBC Weather Waters / Ruth DaviesImage caption, This was the scene above Clawddnewydd in Denbighshire, north WalesImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / LucyImage caption, And this was the picture-perfect view in south west Wales, from Tenby in PembrokeshireImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / ChelseaPhilImage caption, Sightings stretched to Herne Bay in Kent Northern Lights are caused by powerful solar eruptions from the Sun, called coronal mass ejections (CMEs).Towards the end of last week, the Sun was observed to unleash CMEs directed towards the Earth.This stream of charged particles can get captured by the Earth's magnetic field and directed into our atmosphere, especially towards polar regions.When these charged particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen, coloured light is emitted - this is the aurora.Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / Sarah n EssieImage caption, Revellers were able to take in a mix of green and purple in Saltburn-by-the-Sea, North YorkshireImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / HolImage caption, Stenness on Scotland's Orkney Islands served as a strong location for the phenomenonImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / Hannah and BenImage caption, The sky was illuminated in Holmwood, SurreyThe chances of seeing the aurora vary across the UK depending upon its strength. When activity levels reach 200nT (nanotesla) the aurora would be visible in the north of the UK, but not the south.On Saturday evening, those levels reached 600nT, meaning it would be visible across the whole of the UK, even in the south, which is a much rarer phenomenon.Experts have previously said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting as the Sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.Image source, BBC Weather Watchers / Carolyn RImage caption, A purple glow could be seen across the sky in Salisbury, Wiltshire on SaturdayImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / Rick1Image caption, North Yorkshire did not miss out on the action, as shown here in ScarboroughImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / RockdodgerImage caption, An array of pink, blue and green could be seen in Gourock, InverclydeImage source, BBC Weather Watchers / Flower MoonImage caption, The pink and purple hues could also be seen at Llangefni, AngleseyIf you missed out this time, the aurora may return on Sunday.The Met Office has said sightings remain possible across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies until Tuesday.To see them, you need to look northwards, away from bright streetlights, and view the aurora through a mobile phone camera.The reason you need to use a camera is because in low-light conditions at night our eyes use rod cells to see - these cells do not perceive colour and so we actually see in black and white. Cameras do not have the same limitations.

schema.headline: Northern Lights dazzles skies across the UK

title: Why are so many four-year-olds not potty-trained before school?
description: For some parents the countdown to starting school means buying uniforms, labelling water bottles and trying to squeeze in one last summer holiday.For
body: For some parents the countdown to starting school means buying uniforms, labelling water bottles and trying to squeeze in one last summer holiday.For others there is a more basic question to tackle: can their child use the toilet on their own?According to a survey by the charity Kindred Squared, almost a third of children starting school in the West Midlands last year were not fully toilet-trained and 42% of those arriving in reception were deemed not school-ready by primary school staff. This week the charity announced its potty-training scheme, which provides resources and support including increased training for nurseries, schools and professionals, will be rolled out in Solihull. In a pilot in York, which began in April, parents were sent potty-training and school readiness guides with their offers of a school place. Workshops were held, resources distributed and support offered through GPs, pharmacies, libraries and community hubs. As a result, the number of non-toilet-trained children starting reception fell by almost half.Rachel, a mother-of-two from Nottinghamshire, is one of Lue-Quee's clients. She tried to toilet-train her son when he was three but he had problems with withholding stools.She works as a teacher but said being on the other side of the problem as a parent was very different."I'd say as a teacher, I feel I'm quite an informed parent in this area," she said. "So I was thinking, 'I know what's going on but I don't know what to do'."It's not the parent, it's not being lazy; it's hard and it's a lot of effort," she added.She was told she would not be able to access funded support for her child until he was five, and it was not until the end of his reception year that the family received help. Now aged eight, her son is awaiting an assessment for ADHD, which Rachel believes could have affected aspects of his development despite going unnoticed in his early years."Withholding can be trauma-informed and it can be because of passing something that has hurt at some point or someone has reacted badly to them having an accident," she said, adding she believed embarrassment and shame had contributed to her son's difficulties after he had an accident at nursery.Helen Davies, a health visitor and children's nurse based in Stafford, said children who repeatedly had accidents may be frightened of the toilet, leading to constipation."A child who is struggling may be frightened of the toilet, withholding poo or experiencing constipation. Repeated accidents should prompt curiosity about what is getting in the way rather than an assumption that parents have not tried hard enough," she said.Bailey, a former reception teacher and early years lead, said she had worked in "deprived and affluent areas" and had seen inequalities in school readiness."It comes down to income," she said. While some parents were able to buy parenting books, she said those on lower incomes had less access to information."Books are quite expensive," she added, suggesting families could be given free toilet-training resources when their children turned two.Davies, who provides one-to-one guidance through her company Essential Parenting, said families may not be getting "timely, consistent support before difficulties become entrenched".She said financial pressure, parental stress, limited opportunities for play and difficulty accessing early years provision and professional advice could make preparing for school harder."Public services are essential, particularly for families who cannot afford private support," she said.

schema.headline: Why are so many four-year-olds not potty-trained before school?

title: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung
description: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors fou
body: Pope Leo XIV has announced he will be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up."The doctors found an early, well-localised nodule on my lung," he told the public during his weekly Sunday prayers in St Peter's Square in Rome.The 71-year-old said his medical team "believe it would be right to intervene" and he had agreed to the operation, while reassuring pilgrims that the mass was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage".The pontiff's admission that he would need surgery comes nearly a year-and-a-half after he succeeded the late Pope Francis, who also experienced issues with his lungs that required hospital treatment.Leo concluded his Angelus prayer by thanking everyone for their "spiritual closeness" and said he entrusted himself to their prayers.Holy See Press Office spokesman Matteo Bruni told the media that "the operation is scheduled for the first days of next week".He added that the Pope is expected to take about a week to recover.Vatican News, the Holy See's news portal, said the operation will take place at Gemelli Hospital in Rome.The hospital set up a special Papal suite following the failed assassination attempt on Pope John Paul II's life in May 1981, which is still in use today.Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her "personal solidarity" with the Pope as he "faces the ordeal ahead in the coming days".Her sentiments were echoed by Italian President Sergio Mattarella, who offered his "sincerest wishes for a peaceful recovery and a speedy and full return to health".Isaac Herzog, the president of Israel, also wished the pontiff "a full and speedy recovery".The Pope, born Robert Francis Prevost, is the 267th occupant of the throne of St Peter – the first US citizen to do so.He was ordained in 1982 and spent years as a missionary in Peru, where he is remembered as a figure who worked with marginalised communities.During Sunday's service, the Pope confirmed his upcoming visit to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November will still go ahead.The Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla, said preparations for his tour will continue with "greater enthusiasm" as he called for prayers for his recovery.A lung nodule is a small lump of tissue that is usually detected following an X-ray or CT scan of the chest, according to the NHS.Most nodules do not cause other symptoms.

schema.headline: Pope Leo XIV to have surgery after nodule found on lung

title: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant
description: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said i
body: Yandex confirmed on Telegram that its data centre in Vladimir had been damaged and that operations had been "completely suspended", although it said it was working to restore connectivity.The other strikes against Yandex facilities were on Thursday in Sasovo and Friday in in Kaluga, south-west of Moscow, causing problems for some of its services, such as its AI chatbot and smart home devices.The tech company - which also runs a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people - said at the time that its data centres were critical for the normal operation of its services, and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.Meanwhile, Russian strikes on Ukraine have continued through the weekend.The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said six people were injured in Russian attacks overnight on four districts in its south-eastern Dnipropetrovsk region.On Saturday, at least 20 people including four children were killed in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia, local officials confirmed.Russia has previously also struck Ukrainian data centres, causing internet outages and prompting some firms to move their servers abroad.

schema.headline: Yandex: Ukraine strikes data centre in third attack on Russian tech giant

title: Plan 2: Three friends on a decade of student loans
description: Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping upImage source, SuppliedImage caption, Lizzy, Charlotte and Libb
body: Three friends on their student debt: One paid off, one chipping away and one creeping upImage source, SuppliedImage caption, Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby studied at the University of Newcastle between 2012 and 2015ByEducation correspondentWhen Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte met as freshers in 2012, their main responsibility was making it to lectures on time after early morning sports practice.Their student debt, growing with interest from the day they took out their loans, was the last thing on their minds."The conversation was just so much less relevant at that time," says Charlotte. "As our careers have gone on and our paths have diverged more and more... those conversations start to come more to the forefront."The friends, now in their early 30s, went to the University of Newcastle in the same year tuition fees tripled to £9,000 a year in England and Wales, and new loans called Plan 2 were introduced. Each borrowed about £37,500 to cover three years of tuition and living costs.This year marks a decade since the first students in their year started repaying.  They may have started out in the same position, but over that time their career trajectories, life choices and earnings have shaped how much they've repaid, how much interest they've racked up, and how much they owe - with very different outcomes.Student loans have come under scrutiny this year and there's been a particular backlash over Plan 2 loans. The government has said it wants to make the whole system fairer and campaigners are waiting to see what, if anything, changes in this month's Budget.The anger about Plan 2 grew after the government announced updated terms in November. The income at which graduates start repaying is set to be frozen for three years, meaning graduates would start making payments sooner and pay more each month.But it has also been brewing because the interest rate is higher than most other student loan plans, and many have seen their debts rise despite making monthly repayments."Since April this year, I've paid off in the region of £450 and I've accrued over £500 in interest," says Charlotte, a physiotherapist in Bristol.She did a master's degree after uni and worked in the NHS before moving to the private sector. She earns about £50,000, but her loan is still going up."It makes me angry... it's just disheartening."All three friends earn above the national average of £39,039. But research from the Institute for Fiscal Studies, external in February suggests Plan 2 graduates need to earn about £63,000 or more for a loan balance of £50,000 to start going down."I just had no concept that the debt was going to go up," says Libby, who remembers being in tears when her first student loan letter came through after graduating.Now a project manager in a housing association and living in Worcester, she earns £72,000 and says her student loan balance has hovered at about £47,000 for a number of years. But she is currently on maternity leave and knows the interest will continue to accrue while her earnings - and therefore monthly repayments - drop."It feels like I will never pay it off, so it's something that I'm kind of just sucking up until the loan is written off," she says.Her partner did the same course, starting a year before her and before tuition fees near tripled with the introduction of Plan 2 loans.She says it is "so frustrating" that she has to pay out thousands of pounds a year more on her student debt.Current and former students have different student loan plans depending on where they live in the UK and when they went to university. Plan 2 loans were given out in England for a little more than a decade from 2012 and are still issued in Wales.The debt is written off after 30 years.Lizzy, who studied economics and now works in financial services and lives in Bristol, is the highest paid of the friends, who bonded over rowing at university. She earns £85,000 a year and decided last year to clear her student debt by borrowing money from her family instead.She had estimated that, based on her current earnings trajectory, she would repay her loan in 11 years. By paying off her debt in full early she has accrued less interest and hopes to repay her family in four years - saving about £20,000.The amount graduates are voluntarily repaying towards their student loans has been growing. MoneySavingExpert.com founder Martin Lewis has warned that only higher earners could benefit from making voluntary repayments and most should not be "panicked into overpaying".Finance journalist Holly Mead told the BBC it could make sense for those who are confident they will clear the debt and can make "a really significant overpayment" of tens of thousands of pounds, like Lizzy.But smaller voluntary repayments could mean "you're just voluntarily paying more interest that you don't need to pay", she added.Image source, SuppliedImage caption, Lizzy, Charlotte and Libby say they are grateful they met at university and would go back if they had their time againImage source, SuppliedImage caption, The three friends pictured on Charlotte's wedding dayLizzy says she knows there are many "scenarios in which it doesn't pay off" for people to repay it early."I made a gamble on my future self to actually repay it," she says. "I'm in a very privileged position to be able to do that... Buying your way out of the system or not being in at all is in itself a luxury. It buys you freedom."She and Libby finished their A-levels in 2011 but took a year out before going to university - Libby on a gap year, and Lizzy to resit economics after missing the grade she'd hoped for by a single mark.Lizzy says she knew the delay would mean her fees would be higher, but "it was never explained" that the repayment terms would "look and feel very different"."I think that's something that took me probably the best part of 10 years to understand," she adds, noting that her twin sister did start university in 2011 and had less debt as a result."Whether you went to uni in 2012 or 2011 actually financially has a huge impact, and it shouldn't," she says.There's been lots of discussion about what teenagers were told about Plan 2 loans before they took them out. In March, a BBC investigation found the Department for Education (DfE) had compared monthly repayments to £30-a-month phone contracts in presentations at schools in England a decade ago.An inquiry by MPs then concluded that this amounted to "mis-selling" because it was inaccurate for higher earners.Last month, the government said university applicants in England would be given clearer information about student loans before they take them out.Will we ever pay back our student loans?England's controversial Plan 2 student loans have left many graduates frustrated.All three friends follow the Rethink Repayment campaign on social media. It was set up by Oliver Gardner, who says the first Plan 2 borrowers are grappling with competing financial pressures such as getting on the property ladder and starting families."Maybe in your 20s, you can get away without saving as much, potentially. But now people are like, 'we need the savings to do these big things that we want to do with our lives'," he says.The campaign wants a lower Plan 2 interest rate, a lower repayment rate and for the government to reverse that decision to freeze the threshold at £29,385 in England for three years from 2027 - which, while it is not the first freeze, sparked this year's debate.Gardner said the government was "engaging much more openly and honestly" but "the onus is very much on them in the upcoming October budget to take this by the reins" because graduates would not accept "minor tinkering around the edges".The DfE said it was "taking decisive action to improve the student finance system and break down barriers to accessing university"  by increasing maximum maintenance loans, reintroducing targeted maintenance grants and having "raised the repayment threshold for Plan 2 loans for the first time since 2021"."We will continue to look for ways to make the system fairer for students, graduates and taxpayers in a financially sustainable way," it said.Lizzy, Libby and Charlotte feel grateful they met back in 2012, and say that if they had their time again they would go back to university."I still wouldn't change my university experience," says Charlotte, "but would go back and do something different in the sense of my course and my career trajectory? Probably."

schema.headline: Plan 2: Three friends on a decade of student loans

title: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says
description: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migratio
body: At least 139 migrants including 15 children have died and dozens more are still missing after a boat sank off the coast of Djibouti, the UN's migration office has said.The boat had been travelling from Djibouti to Yemen with 305 people aboard when it capsized near the port town of Obock on Thursday night. Around 82 people were rescued, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said.IOM's Djibouti mission chief Alexandre Coissac called the tragedy a "stark reminder" of the dangers migrants face when seeking a new life elsewhere.Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa make the perilous journey each year hoping to reach Gulf countries for safety and work, the agency says.The organisation revised its toll from 109 on Sunday after 30 more bodies were recovered."This is a devastating loss of life," Coissac said. "Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives."Local authorities are also arranging burials for those who have died, while the survivors - all Ethiopian nationals - have medical care readily available to them.Yemen remains engulfed in a devastating civil war that has lasted more than a decade. Despite this conflict - and growing instability across the wider region - migrants still cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait to Yemen driven by poverty, insecurity and the growing impacts of climate change.Since 10 September, the IOM said its Displacement Tracking Matrix had observed more than 20,000 "movements" from Ethiopia to Djibouti.

schema.headline: Djibouti boat capsize: Children among 139 dead with 84 still missing, UN says

title: Riyadh airport attacks another dangerous moment in already tense conflict
description: The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia
body: The attacks on King Khalid Airport in Riyadh mark another dangerous moment in a region that is already fraught with tension and conflict.Saudi Arabia wasn't ready for this. In recent weeks the Houthis have stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabian soil, but their attacks over the past few days have hit the country's critical infrastructure in the form of the capital's main airport, apparently penetrating Saudi air defences with ease.Saturday's attack killed 12 people and hurt more than 300. On Sunday the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said an "unknown projectile" had hit a passenger hall and a cruise missile had been intercepted nearby.The physical damage can be quickly repaired, but the country's reputation as a safe haven of stability is taking a battering.As well as all the airport attacks, the Houthis have sought to take control of strategically significant positions along the Red Sea coast and around the Bab al-Mandeb Strait. This further increases the risk to safe navigation along the vital maritime corridor - although the Yemeni government says it has "secured" the strait.The civil war in Yemen between the country's government - which is internationally recognised and supported by Saudi Arabia - and the Houthis, who are backed by Iran, has been going on for more than a decade. It has left many thousands of people dead and plunged Yemen into one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.It is a complex and often confusing geopolitical conflict, and this latest escalation needs to be seen in the broader context of the tension between Iran, the United States and Israel.Not since the al-Qaeda insurgency of the mid-2000s has the Kingdom faced such a serious threat. The Saudi government overcame that challenge through an effective hearts and minds campaign. Then it weathered the Arab Spring uprisings around the region which saw off leaders in Tunisia, Libya, Egypt and Yemen. It even shrugged off – with some annoyance – an Iranian ballistic missile attack on Riyadh in March.But this is different. Saudi Arabia may have one of the most powerful air forces in the Middle East, and it has been carrying out devastating air strikes on Houthi positions. Despite this, the opposing forces have managed to seize large portions of the country, particularly in the north and west.But the Houthis know exactly where to hit back: at the soft underbelly of the Saudi economy.As part of the "axis of resistance", the Houthis are a vital strategic partner for Iran. From Jizan on the Red Sea to the petrochemical complex at Khurais, the Houthis are delivering explosive drones and missiles with deadly accuracy.The Red Sea shipping route has become increasingly important, because the Strait of Hormuz, on the other side of the Gulf, has still not fully reopened since the US and Iran have failed to reach a deal to end their war.Targeting ships in the Red Sea is another way that the Houthis are trying to exert leverage - the attacks cause global economic damage, which is a key bargaining chip for Tehran.In early September, the White House stated it would not directly intervene in the Yemen conflict, but could provide intelligence support to the Saudis. It later confirmed that it was supplying intelligence and had deployed military experts to Saudi Arabia.However the situation may have taken a new turn following the latest attack on Riyadh, which killed a US citizen.Speaking to reporters, US President Donald Trump called Saturday's attack "terrible" and indicated he may intervene militarily with the Saudis. "We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision. We move very quickly," Trump said.But that now seems unlikely, at least before crucial US midterm elections next month.When he was re-elected in 2024, Trump promised to end America's role in wars around the world. Despite this, the US is currently involved in three unresolved conflicts in the Middle East - in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.Should Trump get embroiled in another one, this time in Yemen, it is unlikely to go down well with voters.This war now looks like it will intensify before it ends in another shaky truce - with or without US involvement.Additional analysis from Abdelbassir Hassan, BBC Arabic

title: Man, 36, arrested six years on from Moss Side double murder
description: A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago.Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff
body: A man has been arrested on suspicion of murder in connection with the fatal shooting of two men more than six years ago.Junior Ajose, 36, and Cheriff Tall, 21, were shot dead at a lockdown party in the Moss Side area of Manchester in the early hours of 21 June 2020.A Greater Manchester Police (GMP) spokesperson said a 36-year-old man was detained in Turkey and transported back to England on Saturday, where he was met at Stansted Airport by GMP officers. He remains in custody.Det Ch Insp Neil Higginson from the force's major incident team said: "This arrest demonstrates our unwavering commitment to securing justice for Junior and Cheriff and their loved ones.""Over the last six years, myself and my officers have been carrying out multiple warrants, analysing evidence, examining devices that have been seized during the investigation and pursuing every opportunity to identify those responsible," he added.Ajose and Tall, who did not know each other, were both shot in the head in a car park off Caythorne Street shortly before 01:00 BST and died in hospital.GMP said it was estimated that between 300 and 400 people were present in the car park that night.The force issued a further appeal for information on the fifth anniversary of their deaths last year.Higginson said they were continuing to appeal for information that could help them to establish the full circumstances of what happened that night and to identify any outstanding suspects.A £50,000 reward remains available for key information that leads to the conviction of the killer.

title: Saudi Arabia's Riyadh airport hit by second Houthi strike in two days
description: An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.A Saudi military spokesman s
body: An international airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh has been hit by a second strike in as many days, officials have said.A Saudi military spokesman said a projectile had hit King Khalid International Airport on Sunday, causing a fire in one of its passenger halls. Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said there had been injuries.It comes a day after a strike on the same airport killed 13 people and injured 308 others, following similar strikes earlier this week.The Houthis in Yemen said they were behind the attacks and warned airlines and passengers against using Saudi Arabian airports and airspace.The group said they had targeted the airport with a mix of ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as drones in the past 24 hours.They also attacked oil facilities and Dammam airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, their military spokesman Brig Gen Yahya Saree said.He vowed to continue the "escalating operations deep inside Saudi Arabia", warning that all Saudi airports were potential targets apart from those in the holy cities of Mecca and Medina.The Houthis have said they are targeting Saudi Arabia over its support for government forces in Yemen's civil war, as well as an air strike on the airport in Sanaa.On Sunday Maj Gen Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition, said air defences had intercepted a missile near the airport in Riyadh, while authorities were dealing with the fire caused by an "unknown projectile" that hit Passenger Hall No 4.US President Donald Trump has said the US would "make a decision" and "move very quickly" on whether to strike the Houthis, while UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting suggested the UK could "potentially" provide more support for Saudi Arabia.

title: I was told I had depression for 14 years until I got sectioned - it was bipolar
description: Prof Danny Smith, chair of psychiatry at the University of Edinburgh, told the BBC  that better "screening" was needed by health professionals, such a
body: Prof Danny Smith, chair of psychiatry at the University of Edinburgh, told the BBC  that better "screening" was needed by health professionals, such as asking about symptoms like mania and if patients had a family history of the condition.His call for screening guidance to be urgently updated is backed by the Royal College of Psychiatrists and charity Bipolar UK.They say better screening could be "life-saving" as medication for depression can often make people with bipolar more unwell.During Kimberley's three-month stay in hospital, psychiatrists looked beyond her depression for the first time. At first she didn't want to accept her bipolar diagnosis but she said years of symptoms eventually made sense. "When I think about how my life was before my diagnosis, it was so chaotic," Kimberley said. "Whereas now I'm stable, which is in large part due to the medication."Jacqui Armstrong also spent years being treated for depression before receiving the correct diagnosis.The 64-year-old began treatment on various antidepressants from her teenage years and over the next three decades her depressions led to several hospital admissions and a suicide attempt, all while she worked as a teacher in a primary school then a nursery."I couldn't even get up the stairs, I was just broken," she said. "I just felt like a huge failure the whole time, thinking 'why can't I get well?'."Jacqui said that during one episode, she was even given electroconvulsive therapy – a treatment that uses an electric current to induce a controlled seizure.But she said the signs of bipolar were always there.As well as frequent depressive periods, she experienced 'hypomania' episodes, spurts of unusually high energy, activity, or mood that were less severe than full mania. "I would suddenly feel like a confident person, and I had all these ideas, and I was very sociable, thinking how many things can I fit into my diary," she said."And then I would energise myself into a breakdown."It was only during her final hospital admission for depression that a psychiatrist asked Jacqui if she'd ever experienced symptoms of hypomania. She was then assessed further and diagnosed her with bipolar II – more than 30 years after first seeking help for her mental health.Meanwhile Kimberley, who had experienced a "full" manic episode that resulted in a break from reality, was diagnosed with bipolar I.Experts say bipolar II is even harder to diagnose because it involves more frequent depressions and the manic episodes are not as severe, which is why they are dubbed hypomania.Experts such as Smith believe bipolar disorder is significantly underdiagnosed.He said about one in 100 people receive a diagnosis during their lifetime but research suggests the true figure could be closer to one in 50.Studies also suggest patients in the UK typically wait almost a decade between first reporting symptoms and receiving a diagnosis. Smith said the long delays suggest that people are not being routinely screened properly for symptoms of hypomania or mania which should result in a referral to a psychiatrist to rule out the possibility of bipolar.While existing UK-wide guidelines, external say doctors should already do this, Smith said updated and better-publicised screening tools are "really important" because research suggests this is routinely not happening."It's understandable because GPs are often confronted with depressed patients and therefore they're very focused on diagnosing depression correctly," he said."People obviously don't go to the GP and say 'Help doctor, I'm really energetic and I've got lots of ideas and I don't need much sleep.'"While awareness for the condition has increased in recent years – with high-profile figures like Stephen Fry and Chappell Roan being public in their diagnosis – charity Bipolar UK said too little attention is being paid to the illness, and delayed diagnosis is "costing lives".Smith said it's important the public knows that bipolar is a "highly manageable" condition when diagnosed, and that people who get proper treatment can "do really well" with normal families and successful careers.Both Kimberley and Jacqui were prescribed various antidepressant medications over the years to little or no benefit - but never asked if they had experienced mania until they reached the point of hospitalisation."It's scary," Kimberley said. "I would never have thought that I would end up behaving in the way that I had, and I can't imagine being that way now."Now she has the right diagnosis, she said she's doing much better.She is currently working full-time as an assistant psychologist for the NHS, and hasn't had a manic episode since she was sectioned four years ago.Jacqui has described the last few years as her "happiest in a long time"."I've brought up two children with my husband and had a career, but I just now for the first time feel properly me," she said."I don't feel embarrassed about my diagnosis like I know some people do."I just feel gosh, if I was diabetic, I wouldn't be embarrassed. It's about getting the right help."If you or someone you know have been affected the issues in the story, you can find more information about organisations that can help at BBC Action Line.

title: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after fatal tiger attack
description: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal. Emergency services were call
body: Yorkshire Wildlife Park remains closed after a man climbed into a tiger enclosure and was fatally attacked by the animal. Emergency services were called to the park near Doncaster, South Yorkshire, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday after reports of a man climbing down into the enclosure from a walkway. An eyewitness described seeing the man wearing headphones and "pacing around" near the enclosure before he went in and was attacked. Police said the man sadly died at the scene. A park spokesperson said their "thoughts and heartfelt sympathies" remain with the man's family and confirmed the Amur tiger, called Altai, remained in the enclosure and would not be euthanised.The spokesperson says many people had contacted them about the tiger and he was safe and well. Staff who were at the scene who were "deeply affected by events" would receive specialist support, they added.South Yorkshire Police said the man's family were being supported by officers. "Our thoughts are with them at this distressing time," the force said in a statement. It added: "We are aware of videos circulating online and we would encourage people not to share this footage."Earlier on Saturday, in a statement posted on its website, the park said its emergency response procedures had been "immediately activated" and it was "working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened".Ella Ford, 24, from Moreton, Wirral, had visited the park with her boyfriend and filmed the tiger moments before the attack. She described seeing a man by the tiger enclosure "pacing around with his headphones in".A few minutes later, she saw the same man had "climbed up onto the barriers".A woman was close by talking to him, she said, before "he jumped in and crawled in front of the tiger, where the tiger was perched and just lay there".Ford said she then witnessed the tiger grab hold of the man, who she reported as "shouting for help".She estimates around 15 to 20 people were on the enclosure's raised visitor walkway before staff quickly evacuated the area, and shortly afterwards, the park.She described members of the public as being "confused, like what on earth's going on?""I just know some man was obviously trying to bang on the fence to try and deter the tiger away, but it obviously wasn't doing anything," she said.Karmelle Pelham, 39, from Worksop, had been enjoying a family day out when park staff told them the site was being evacuated.She said she had heard what sounded like "gunshots" and an air ambulance had circled above.Pelham added: "There was a big, black tarpaulin over the tiger enclosure." She praised park staff for their handling of the incident, saying it had been "very, very well organised".Foreign Secretary and MP for Doncaster North Ed Miliband said he was "deeply saddened" to hear of the incident and sent his "thoughts and deepest condolences to the family of the individual who died."He added he was "very grateful to the emergency services and staff of the park who responded."Lee Pitcher, MP for Doncaster East and the Isle of Axholme, expressed his gratitude to emergency services for their response.In a statement shared to social media, he said he was "deeply saddened to hear about the tragic incident that has taken place at Yorkshire Wildlife Park today".Yorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with its Land of the Tigers area opening in 2011.The purpose-built two-acre reserve is home to Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with around 500 left in the wild.Photos of the enclosure on the park's website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.Additional reporting by James Kelly
